title: Wikramanayake exits Macquarie, APRA slams 'serious' governance failure
full_text:
APRA has slammed Macquarie Group's leadership on the day chief executive Shemara Wikramanayake officially bows out for "a serious failure" in complying with another capital requirement.
Wikramanayake leaves the group souring the prudential regulator for Macquarie having understated the required capital it was expected to hold within its non-bank business during a recent capital review.
The breach dates back to 2019, resulting in lower-than-required capital levels for the non-bank business.
APRA slapped Macquarie Bank with a $100 million governance buffer, which is on top of the $500 million capital overlay already in place, dating back to 2021. That related to the incorrect treatment of specific intra-group funding arrangements when calculating capital and related entity exposure metrics, as well as multiple breaches of APRA's reporting standards on liquidity between 2018 and 2020.
APRA deputy chair Therese McCarthy Hockey commented the new breach reflected "a serious failure in Macquarie Group's governance and assurance processes."
"While APRA acknowledges Macquarie's cooperation, addressing the breach after identification does not diminish the seriousness of the underlying failure. Board and senior executives are responsible for ensuring their institutions maintain effective risk management, assurance and governance practices that support compliance, not simply react when deficiencies are identified," she said.
APRA's action comes as Wikramanayake departs after nearly 40 years with the group.
Wikramanayake took over the top spot in December 2018 from Nicholas Moore.
In its half-year results for the period ended September 30, Macquarie Group announced a net profit after tax of $2.5 billion, up 50% year on year.
Macquarie Asset Management's (MAM) net profit jumped 28% year on year to $1.5 billion driven by higher net investment income stemming from the sale of Macquarie AirFinance and a higher share of net profits from associates and joint ventures from various asset sales.
On its capital management and funding position for the bank, Macquarie boasted its financial position exceeds APRA's Basel III regulatory requirements.
The banking unit's Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) capital ratio was 12.9%, up from 12.8% from March, while its leverage ratio 4.4% and liquidity coverage ratio was 187%.
"The strength of the result reflects the diversity of our businesses, the depth of our expertise to navigate less certain market conditions and our teams' ability to identify opportunities and deliver for our clients," Wikramanayake said.
"It has been a privilege to work with so many talented Macquarie teams over the last 39 years, including for the last eight years as chief executive, and I have every confidence in the momentum continuing under Greg Ward's leadership."
Greg Ward was named as Wikramanayake's successor, taking the post officially on November 7.
The next steps include APRA overseeing a full assessment of Macquarie's approach to determining the required capital for its non-bank business. Depending on the assessment findings, APRA warned it may consider further action.
"Macquarie is one of the country's largest financial groups and, as such, APRA expects it to have among the highest standards of governance, risk management and controls. Macquarie failed to identify and address this issue through its own governance and assurance processes, which falls short of APRA's expectations," McCarthy Hockey said.
author: Karren Vergara
